title: King
brief_context: Rebuilt the fortress on Castle Rock in 7th century.
article_title: EDINBURGH —venue for the EAW Annual Conference
brief_extract: The Castle Rock which dominates the town and has dominated the history of Scotland from earliest times is of volcanic origin. Edwin, King of Northumbria, rebuilt the fortress on the Rock in the seventh century after a successful invasion and gave his name to the township which began to grow up around it. The small chapel on the Rock which is Edinburgh's oldest building was built in the eleventh century by Queen Margaret, wife of Malcolm III who was the son of the Duncan who was murdered by Macbeth.

brief_context: Visited Moray House.
article_title: EDINBURGH —venue for the EAW Annual Conference
brief_extract:
A walk down from the Castle Esplanade to the Palace is highly to be recommended as it takes us past some of the oldest and best preserved buildings in Edinburgh including St. Giles' Cathedral, John Knox's House with its ancient timber galleries dating from the fifteenth century, Moray House where Charles I visited and Cromwell made his Headquarters, Canon-gate Church in whose churchyard Adam Smith is buried, Huntly House now an interesting museum of local history, and many fascinating closes and wynds which still give us an im-pression of what the busy congested Royal Mile was like when it was the main thoroughfare of the city before the New Town was built. 18th Century New Town
The rudiments of town planning were apparent in Edinburgh during the seventeenth century when the growth of the population in the Old Town huddled around the Mount and straggling along the Royal Mile made it necessary to house people in high buildings, some of which exist to this day.

brief_extract: The power station is in the heart of the mountain. by GEORGE BANKS, Information Officer, North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board. THE Hydro-Electric Development (Scotland) Bill which set up the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board in 1943 was a piece of far-sighted planning to be introduced in those war-torn years, and was more than mere legislation to permit the fuller development of a great natural resource, the water-power of Highland lochs and rivers, by a public authority.

title: Mrs
role: wife of the Secretary of State
brief_context: Performed a sod-cutting ceremony using a bulldozer.
brief_extract: Instead of the traditional polished spade there was an 18-ton bulldozer, the sod was a 12-feet wide strip of turf 100 feet long, and the job, the first step in a continuous drive to build dams, power stations and supply networks throughout the North, was the Loch Sloy hydro-electric scheme whose great dam and power station were to draw visitors from all over the world and become a kind of symbol of post-war Scotland. The lady who found herself perched high in the driving seat of the bulldozer was Mrs Margaret Johnston, wife of the Secretary of State, who, like so many of her generation, shared her husband’s enthusiasm for this effort to improve the economy of the Highlands. That brief and bumpy trip across the turf was for her but the prelude to many hundreds of miles at the wheel to assist hydro-electric development, for after Mr Johnston retired from politics and became chairman of the Board in 1946 she drove him for many years all over the North to visit constructional work and inspect the sites of future projects.

title: Mr
brief_context: Creator of the garden at Inverewe starting in 1862.
brief_extract: To walk through this garden one would find it difficult to believe that in 1862 this was a barren rocky wind-swept peninsula. The creator of this paradise, Mr Osgood MacKenzie, required years of painstaking methodical planting to lay the foundations of the beautiful garden we see today. First he established a shelter belt that would stand up to the lashing of the winter gales, then gradually as the shelter belt grew it was possible to plant less hardy subjects the range of which needs ten pages of the official guide book to list.

brief_context: Author of the book 'Great Gardens of Britain'.

It is strange that Peter Coats in his book 'Great Gardens of Britain' makes no mention of Inverewe. One must assume that he did not bother to venture as far north as the 60th parallel.

brief_context: Founder who set up a grocery shop in 1869.
brief_extract: It could well be likened to the story of the stout oak which grew from the tiny acorn. It all started in 1869, when George Baxter set up a small grocery shop in Spey Street, Fochabers. Jam making started up in the back shop for sale in the front shop.

brief_context: George Baxter's son who expanded the business into jam manufacturing.
brief_extract: This was the simple beginning. When George Baxter's son, William, married in 1914 he and his wife Ethel were quick to see the possibilities in making jams on a grander scale and selling them to retail shops, but it was impossible to increase production in the confines of a grocery shop and, being enterprising people, they naturally wished to work on their own account. William, therefore, approached the local landowner, the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, and secured a plot of land near the Spey on which to build their own small jam factory, and it was indeed a great day for them when they started production there in 1916.

brief_context: Son of William and Ethel who runs the business today.
brief_extract:
Twentieth-Century Romance from Speyside
SPEYSIDE—yes, that fair land in North-east Scotland where you can live like a laird on the fine natural foods of this bountiful countryside—salmon from the rushing, tumbling waters of the River Spey, succulent wild duck from the Loch of Spynie, plump pheasant and partridge, hare and prime venison from the sporting estates, soft fruit and vegetables from the fertile Laich of Moray—and all of these have truly been captured for the whole world to enjoy by BAXTERS OF SPEYSIDE throughout their wonderful range of delightful soups, mouth-watering casseroles, canned fruits and jams. That go-ahead company, with its international ramifications, is still a family-owned concern, a rare thing in these days of manufacturing giants and takeover bids. Their policy today is the same as it was when the business first started over a hundred years ago to produce and market only the finest quality Scottish products.

brief_context: Husband of Ena and co-founder of the Baxter soup company.
brief_extract: The Baxter family has always been fortunate in the women they married. Gordon’s wife, Ena, has played a particularly important part in the company’s development. Shortly after their marriage she saw a recipe for Louisiana Chicken Gumbo soup in the American magazine ‘Gourmet’.

brief_context: Remains involved in product development and recipe testing.
brief_extract:
Baxter’s experimental kitchen

Original Baxter shop

The Baxter policy of uncompromisingly high quality and innovation is pursued as keenly as ever—this is their yardstick, and despite ever-increasing competition as many of the giants now realise there may be something in it for them too in this very worthwhile market, and others are quick to imitate, this company can be said to be the fastest growing soup company in Europe. Ena Baxter remains closely involved with all new product development, trying out new recipes in her own kitchen at home. If her family like them and she herself is satisfied, the idea may then be further developed in the experimental kitchen and put through exhaustive tests until a product is arrived at which is approved by the Baxter family and their Executive Tasting Panel.

In Cramond Kirk is Queen Victoria's chair, reminder of the pre-Balmoral days when queen and court sought peace and quiet in Scotland. Among the marks of modern life in Cramond none is as plain or as unobtrusive as is electricity.

title: Miss; CBE
brief_context: Director of EAW awarded a CBE in Birthday Honours.
brief_extract: Since jubilation is really related to a jubilee the EAW has had very good cause to celebrate and the excitement all started with the launching of the EAW Golden Jubilee Year at the unforgettable conference in Scotland. Another cause for EAW rejoicing was the award of the CBE to Miss Mary George in the Birthday Honours List. While members were delighted at this honour given to their Director at any time, it was a special pleasure that it should have been conferred in this very special EAW year.

title: Mr
associated_organisation: National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting
brief_context: Contributor discussing electrical wiring and the home environment.
brief_extract: Delegates to the Edinburgh Conference had the privilege of listening to an animated discussion on electricity and the environment, and in this issue of the magazine Miss George presents the main points considered. Mr Kinloch of the National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting shows how electrical wiring makes its contribution to the home environment. Conservation of energy is now the national watchword and the EAW which has always urged the economic and advantageous use of electricity in the home will be even more active in presenting its own members and the public with the information needed to use electricity in the most efficient way.

title: CBE; Companion IEE
brief_context: Author of the article and chair of the discussion panel.
brief_extract:
Electricity

and the

Environment

by MARY GEORGE, CBE, Companion IEE
Director EAW

Audience for EAW discussion

OUR current campaign theme ‘Electricity’s
Contribution towards a Better Environ-
ment’ can be tackled from so many ways
that it was especially valuable to hear the points
of view of four experts in their own fields. I had
the pleasure of chairing the discussion in Edin-
burgh and noting with the audience the truth of
the old Latin tag ‘quot homines tot sententiae’
—many men, many minds.

title: Mr
brief_context: Confirmed cultivation limitations near undergrounded high voltage cables.
brief_extract:
Underground cables
The panel then discussed the siting of cables, both overhead and underground, with particular reference to the effect on cultivation resulting from undergrounding cables in rural areas of high natural beauty. Mr Tombs confirmed that where very high voltage cables were undergrounded no trees could be planted and there could be little cultivation since a 30 ft wide access path per circuit had to be provided. With lower voltage cables normal cultivation was possible.

title: Mr
brief_context: Spoke about landscape architecture problems with overhead cables.
brief_extract: With lower voltage cables normal cultivation was possible. Mr Gillespie spoke of the problems for the landscape architect in dealing with overhead cables, and said that trenching also produced problems since disturbed soil resulted and the ground did not recover its normal appearance for a long time. Mrs Murray Leishman and Mr Reid struck an encouraging note, the former by referring to the undergrounding of cables in show villages in Fife and Cromarty, and the latter stating that the electricity authorities should not be blamed for all overhead cables, since these were also needed for telephones and television.
